title: Why you wake up at 3am
description: So many perimenopausal women wake at almost exactly the same hour that it can't be a coincidence. Here's what's actually happening in the body.
coverImageAlt: Woman lying awake in bed in the early hours, eyes open in the dark

slides.headline: You fall asleep fine. Then, like a switch flips.
slides.body: Somewhere between 2:30 and 3:30am, your eyes open. Not gradually — suddenly. Your mind is instantly, unhelpfully alert. If this happens to you most nights, you're far from alone.

slides.headline: It's not a coincidence, and it isn't "just stress"
slides.body: Ask around perimenopause communities and you'll find women comparing notes on the exact hour their body wakes them — as if it were a scheduled appointment nobody remembers booking.

slides.headline: Falling progesterone loses its calming effect
slides.body: Progesterone has a natural, sleep-supporting effect on the brain. As it declines through perimenopause, that nightly calming effect weakens — especially in the second half of the night.

slides.headline: Cortisol rises earlier than it should
slides.body: Add a shifting overnight cortisol rhythm and small overnight blood-sugar dips, both of which can trigger a stress-hormone wake-up call right in the early hours.

slides.headline: Usually it's two or three causes, overlapping
slides.body: Oestrogen changes also disrupt body-temperature regulation, affecting your deepest sleep stages. It's rarely one single cause — which is exactly why it helps to know what's really going on.
